# The project

## What is the goal of the project?

The goal of this project is to build a model that predicts how likely a tweet is to contain offensive, derogatory, or hateful language.
We will train several machine-learning models, compare their performance using AUC,
and use the best-performing model to create predictions for the competition test data.

## Where do the data come from? (To which population will results generalize?)

The dataset consists of tweets and comments from other social media platforms that may contain offensive or derogatory language.
Before use, the text was standardized through extensive preprocessing:
hyperlinks, user mentions, and special characters were removed; contractions were expanded;
emojis were converted to text; misspelled profanities were corrected; and all text was lowercased.
Labels (1 == offensive; 0 == non-offensive) were assigned partly by human annotators and partly by predictive models.

Generalizability is limited in several ways. The dataset was class-balanced to a 1:1 ratio of offensive to non-offensive content,
so predicted probabilities do not reflect real-world base rates.
The aggressive preprocessing means the model may perform worse on raw, unprocessed text.
Finally, machine-generated labels introduce noise and may carry the biases of the model that produced them.

## What are candidate machine learning methods? (models? features?)

Regularized logistic regression is a good starting point because it works well with large, sparse text-feature matrices.
Candidate models include lasso, ridge, and elastic-net logistic regression,
which regularize the many word n-gram, character-shingle, and extra tweet-level features.
Tree-based methods are also of interest because they can capture nonlinear relationships and interactions.
XGBoost gradient-boosted decision trees are therefore a promising additional candidate.
Methods such as Naïve Bayes, PLS, PCA, and standard random forests are less suitable because the feature matrix is
extremely high-dimensional and sparse.
Other techniques that we didn't study in the course so far, but some approaches that would be interesting in principle
are support vector machines or the integration of Transformer models.

## What is the Bayes' error bound?

The Bayes error rate cannot be identified from this dataset alone.
Both human annotators and predictive models made labelling errors: humans disagree on borderline cases,
miss sarcasm, or misjudge context-dependent insults,
while machine-generated labels inherit the biases and errors of the model that produced them.
This irreducible label noise implies a Bayes error above zero.
In terms of AUC, the theoretical ceiling is 1.0, but given labelling noise the practical ceiling is likely lower.
A realistic upper bound on achievable AUC might lie somewhere between 0.95 and 0.98, with the remainder being irreducible noise.
